Neonatal stress alters transcriptional pathways involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, mitophagy and dynamics within respiratory brainstem regions, revealing persistent molecular remodelling associated with early-life adversity.

title: Pregnancy Outcomes Following Maternal Exposure to Pramipexole: A TERAFAR Case Series.
abstract: To evaluate pregnancy outcomes following maternal pramipexole exposure using data from the Izmir Kâtip Celebi University Teratology Information, Training and Research Center (TERAFAR). Pregnant women exposed to pramipexole and referred to the TERAFAR between 2011 and 2025 were evaluated. Maternal demographic data, medical history, and exposure details were recorded at the initial visit; pregnancy outcomes and neonatal data were collected through postpartum telephone interviews. The primary outcome was the rate of major congenital malformations, while secondary outcomes included miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth, and low birth weight. A total of 11 pregnancies were evaluated. Median maternal age was 36 years, and restless legs syndrome was the primary indication in 10 of the 11 pregnancies. The median daily dose was 0.25 mg. Of the 11 pregnancies, 10 resulted in live births and one ended in miscarriage. No major congenital malformations were observed. A minor congenital anomaly (infantile hemangioma) was detected in only one premature infant. In this case series, maternal exposure to pramipexole was not associated with a consistent pattern of congenital anomalies suggestive of a teratogenic signal. Given the clinical context, the minor anomaly observed (infantile hemangioma) is more likely attributable to prematurity and maternal factors than to pramipexole exposure. Given the small sample size, findings should be interpreted with caution but may inform individualized counseling of pregnant women with inadvertent pramipexole exposure. Further studies are warranted.

title: Evaluating plasma phosphorylated tau217 for clinical rule-out of cerebral amyloid pathology: Evidence from a memory clinic cohort.
abstract: BackgroundPlasma phosphorylated tau 217 (pTau217) is a promising biomarker for Alzheimer's disease amyloid-β (Aβ) pathology, but cut-offs require validation.ObjectiveThe aim was to evaluate the diagnostic performance of plasma phosphorylated tau 217 for identifying cerebral amyloid pathology to reduce the need for more invasive or resource-intensive confirmatory testing by identifying individuals with a low likelihood of amyloid pathology.MethodsElecsys® pTau217 was evaluated in a memory clinic cohort using ROC analysis. Cut-offs were derived using sensitivity-weighted Euclidean distance and bootstrap resampling.ResultspTau217 discriminated Aβ-positive from Aβ-negative individuals (AUC 0.854). The cut-off was 0.169 pg/mL (95% CI 0.140-0.200), with 87.7% sensitivity and 77.0% specificity. Age and sex adjustment did not improve performance.ConclusionsThe threshold was consistent with previously reported low cut-offs, supporting potential rule-out utility; however, its sensitivity precludes stand-alone exclusion of Aβ pathology in memory clinic populations.

title: Metabolite profiling of a Bolboschoenus planiculmis extract and its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and enzyme inhibitory properties with potential for skin health applications.
abstract: In this study, we aimed to evaluate a 70 % ethanol extract of B. planiculmis (BPEE) for its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and skin aging-related enzyme inhibitory activities, and conduct non-targeted metabolite profiling using UPLC-QTOF-MS/MS. BPEE exhibited concentration-dependent antioxidant capacity, as demonstrated by DPPH and ABTS radical scavenging activities, and ferric reducing antioxidant power, consistent with its polyphenol and flavonoid content. In lipopolysaccharide-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages, BPEE showed no cytotoxicity and significantly suppressed nitric oxide, prostaglandin E2, and interleukin-1β production in a concentration-dependent manner. Furthermore, BPEE inhibited key skin aging-related enzymes, including tyrosinase, collagenase, and elastase, with kinetic analyses revealing distinct inhibition patterns for each enzyme. UPLC-QTOF-MS/MS analysis identified a diverse array of metabolites, including flavonoids, stilbenes, triterpenoids, and lipid-derived compounds, many of which have been reported to possess antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and extracellular matrix-protective properties, providing a plausible chemical context for the observed activities. Collectively, these findings characterize the in vitro activity profile of BPEE and provide a basis for further investigation of B. planiculmis. Its relevance to skin health should be established through evaluation in skin-derived cell and tissue models.

title: Presynaptic CAST Deficiency Disrupts Neural Regulation and Promotes Restlessness and Depression-Like Behaviors.
abstract: In modern society, diverse stressful environments are recognized as major social problems because they increase vulnerability to psychiatric disorders and depression. Stress responses are mediated by distributed neural circuits, including cortico-limbic and brainstem networks, in which the hypothalamus acts as a central hub regulating circadian rhythms, parental care, and feeding behavior through modulation of neurotransmission. Presynaptic active zone scaffold proteins, including Cytomatrix at the Active Zone-Associated Structural Protein (CAST), are essential for neurotransmitter release, and disruption of their function may contribute to stress-related pathology. Previous studies have reported that CAST knockout (KO) mice exhibit abnormal maternal behaviors and altered sucrose preference, suggestive of depression-like phenotypes. In this study, continuous 24-h home-cage monitoring revealed pronounced restlessness in the locomotor activity of CAST KO mice. Furthermore, the tail suspension test revealed increased immobility in CAST KO mice, consistent with a depression-like state. The administration of a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor reduced immobility in CAST KO mice, suggesting that CAST deficiency increases susceptibility to depression-like behaviors. Collectively, these findings highlight a critical role for CAST in presynaptic neuromodulator release and in modulating vulnerability to stress-induced depressive behaviors.

title: Expression of Tachykinin 2/Neurokinin B and Neuropeptide Y and the Functional Contribution of Neuropeptide Y in the Mouse Dentate Gyrus following Repeated Electroconvulsive Seizure.
abstract: Electroconvulsive therapy is an effective treatment option for major depression. Studies using rodent electroconvulsive seizure (ECS) models have suggested that the dentate gyrus (DG) of the hippocampal formation is critically involved and that ECS induces robust transcriptomic changes in the DG. Although previous studies have suggested that the expression of two neuropeptide genes, Tachykinin 2 (TAC2) and neuropeptide Y (Npy), is induced by repeated ECS in the DG, the temporal and spatial expression patterns of these genes and their functional contribution to the DG remain unknown. In this study, we found that Tac2 mRNA expression was induced by repeated ECS in the subgranular zone (SGZ), a neurogenic niche, of the DG. In contrast, the expression of Npy mRNA was induced by single and repeated ECS in the hilus. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed that repeated ECS increased the number of NPY-positive cells exhibiting low or undetectable somatostatin expression in the hilus, suggesting the presence of a stimulus-responsive cell population. We further found that the ECS-induced increase in immature neurons in the SGZ was partially suppressed by intracerebroventricular infusion of the NPY-Y1 receptor antagonist, suggesting a modulatory role for NPY-Y1 signaling in ECS-induced neurogenesis. These findings suggest that ECS engages neuropeptide-mediated neuromodulation in a distinct temporal and spatial pattern in the DG.

title: Microglia in Psychiatric Disorders: Stage-Dependent Roles and Therapeutic Implications.
abstract: Psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia, mood disorders, and neurodevelopmental disorders, arise from complex interactions between genetic vulnerability and environmental exposures and have traditionally been viewed as diseases resulting from neuronal abnormalities. In recent years, however, growing evidence has highlighted the critical role of non-neuronal cells-particularly microglia-in the pathogenesis of these conditions. Microglia are the resident immune cells of the central nervous system and play essential roles in shaping neural circuits through synaptic pruning and formation. Importantly, microglial functions are not static; they are dynamically regulated in a stage-dependent manner across prenatal, postnatal, and adolescent periods, and disruption at each stage confers distinct risks for psychiatric pathology. In this review, we summarize recent evidence implicating microglia in the pathophysiology of psychiatric disorders, with particular emphasis on how the developmental stage at which microglial dysfunction occurs determines the timing and nature of disease onset. Furthermore, we discuss the therapeutic potential of pharmacological interventions targeting microglial functions in a stage-dependent manner.

title: Safety Assessment of Spirulina Intake on Cytochrome P450 3A-Mediated Drug Metabolism: A Comprehensive Study from an In Vitro Study to a Human Clinical Trial.
journal: Journal of nutritional science and vitaminology
abstract: Spirulina has been gaining increasing attention as a dietary supplement, yet its potential to induce food-drug interactions when taken alongside medications remains insufficiently understood. Inhibition of cytochrome P450 3A (CYP3A), a major drug-metabolizing enzyme, is of concern, as it may play a key role in adverse effect development. Therefore, we aimed to determine whether spirulina induces food-drug interactions through CYP3A inhibition. To assess the inhibitory effects of spirulina on CYP3A activity, midazolam was used as a probe substrate. The inhibitory effects of spirulina and its main components were examined in vitro on midazolam 1'-hydroxylation activity in human liver microsomes. In vivo, rats received a single oral dose of spirulina powder before midazolam administration, and serum midazolam concentrations were compared with those of a control group. A clinical study was also conducted in six healthy Japanese men to examine the effects of short-term, repeated spirulina tablet intake on serum midazolam concentrations in an open-label, two-period, fixed-sequence design. The in vitro results revealed that spirulina inhibited midazolam 1'-hydroxylation activity in a concentration-dependent manner. Among its major components, phycocyanin exhibited weak inhibition, whereas chlorophyll a, zeaxanthin, and β-carotene showed no significant effects. In rats, the AUC0-∞ of midazolam tended to increase by approximately 25% following spirulina administration. However, in the clinical trial, no significant changes were observed in the AUC0-8 or Cmax of midazolam. These findings suggest that short-term spirulina intake is unlikely to cause substantial CYP3A inhibition, though further studies are warranted to fully rule out minor interactions.

title: Molecular Protective Actions of Myricetin against Interleukin-1β-Mediated Cytotoxicity in RINm5F β-Cells by Both Modulating Apoptosis and Inhibiting iNOS Expression Mechanisms.
journal: Journal of nutritional science and vitaminology
abstract: Myricetin, one of the flavonoids, has diverse beneficial effects in β-cells of pancreatic islet. Meanwhile, interleukin-1β (IL-1β), a main pro-inflammatory cytokine, is a key molecule leading to β-cell dysfunction. This study explores protective molecular mechanisms of myricetin against IL-1β-induced β-cells damage. In RINm5F β-cells, IL-1β decreased cell viability, and it increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and nitric oxide (NO). These phenomena were revered by myricetin treatment. Myricetin (30 μM) restored cell viability by reducing apoptosis, modulating the expression of apoptotic molecules, and inhibiting ROS accumulation. Myricetin inhibited IL-1β-induced NO generation, iNOS protein and mRNA expressions in a dose-dependent manner. Additionally, myricetin significantly suppressed IL-1β-mediated IκB phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of NF-κB, a key transcription factor necessary for iNOS transcription and it reduced IL-1β-mediated NF-κB reporter luciferase activity. Consistent with these findings, myricetin significantly inhibited IL-1β-induced iNOS promoter activity at transcriptional step. Interestingly, myricetin meaningfully deteriorated iNOS mRNA stability in actinomycin D chase and iNOS 3'-UTR construct studies at post-transcriptional step. Furthermore, cycloheximide chase study showed that myricetin accelerated iNOS protein instability at post-translational step. Our study suggests that myricetin can protect RINm5F β-cells exposed to IL-1β by inhibiting the apoptotic pathway and in particular, the inhibitory effect of myricetin on iNOS expression is exerted through at transcriptional, post-transcriptional, and post-translational control mechanisms. These results support that myricetin may have a protective effect against pancreatic β-cells dysfunction exposed to proinflammatory cytokine though this study was conducted in in vitro cell line.

title: Integrated clinical and transcriptomic analysis reveals miRNA-mediated mechanisms linking hearing loss to cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: BackgroundHearing loss (HL) is a potent, modifiable risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD), but the underlying molecular mechanisms remain elusive. microRNAs (miRNAs) are potential key mediators given their roles in both neurodegeneration and auditory function.ObjectiveTo investigate whether peripheral blood miRNA profiles differ between AD patients with and without HL, and whether hsa-miR-6875-5p serves as a candidate molecular link.MethodsIn a case-control study of 41 AD patients (AD-HL n = 24, AD-non-HL n = 17), we performed neuropsychological assessments, plasma miRNA sequencing, target gene prediction, and external validation using public transcriptomic datasets.ResultsAD-HL patients showed significantly worse Montreal Cognitive Assessment and Auditory Verbal Learning Test delayed recall scores (p < 0.05). We identified 9 differentially expressed miRNAs, with hsa-miR-6875-5p being the most upregulated (3.29-fold, p = 0.041). Its predicted targets were enriched in synaptic plasticity-related pathways. External validation in AD brain datasets supported consistent upregulation of hsa-miR-6875-5p and downregulation of SYN1/PSD95. Validation in mouse cochlear datasets showed concordant expression trends for homologous miRNA and target genes. The absence of healthy control groups precludes determination of whether this miRNA signature is specific to AD-HL or a general feature of HL or AD.ConclusionsThis preliminary study identifies hsa-miR-6875-5p as a potential circulating biomarker linking HL to cognitive decline in AD. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger cohorts, including healthy controls, and functional experiments.

title: Post-Traumatic Amnesia Testing for Suspected Concussion in the Emergency Department: A Retrospective Study.
abstract: Among patients discharged from the ED after mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), 16%-25% experience post-concussive symptoms for up to 3 months after injury. However, the assessment of mTBI in the ED is variable. A common tool for the assessment of mTBI in Australia is the Abbreviated Westmead Post-Traumatic Amnesia Scale (A-WPTAS). The aim of this study was to report the proportion of patients who were detected to have post-traumatic amnesia (PTA) following a head injury and whether this varied by reported loss of consciousness (LOC), age, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and mechanisms of injury. This was a single-centre, retrospective cohort study. Data were extracted from patients' electronic medical records. All patients presenting to the ED between 1 January 2019 and 31 December 2021 with a head injury, documented results of A-WPTAS, and aged ≥ 18 years were included for analysis. There were 6259 patients included, and 5746 (91.8%, 95% CI: 91.1%-92.5%) passed the A-WPTAS. -PTA was more frequent among patients who presented with GCS 13 or 14, male patients, those with low falls and presenting after hours. Among patients with documented LOC, the pass rate was 90.6% (95% CI: 88.8%-92.4%), and among those without LOC, it was 92% (95% CI: 91.3%-92.8%); p = 0.13. PTA was detected in a small proportion of patients tested in the ED. PTA was associated with low initial GCS, but not with reported LOC. Among patients discharged from the ED, follow-up for persistent post-concussion symptoms is indicated.

title: Scaling a multimodal mind-body movement intervention for Veterans with dementia in VA nursing homes: A formative evaluation of the Preventing Loss of Independence through Exercise (PLIÉ) program.
abstract: BackgroundPeople living with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias constitute a substantial proportion of residents in U.S. Veterans Health Administration nursing homes (Community Living Centers, CLCs). Non-pharmacologic interventions have demonstrated positive effects for people living with dementia (PLWD) but face implementation barriers in nursing homes. The Preventing Loss of Independence through Exercise (PLIÉ) program is an evidence-based multimodal mind-body movement program that supports quality of life and function for PLWD.ObjectiveTo identify potential facilitators and barriers that may impact implementation of PLIÉ in CLCs (PLIÉ-CLC) and inform the development of a remote staff training program.MethodsWe conducted a developmental formative evaluation using qualitative methods, guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR). Semi-structured interviews with 30 CLC staff, directors, and VA health system leaders, explored perspectives on implementing PLIÉ-CLC. Data were analyzed using a template analysis approach.ResultsKey facilitators included PLIÉ's evidence base, adaptability, and alignment with person-centered care. Barriers included staffing constraints, workload demands, and limited accessible space. Participants emphasized the need for both synchronous and asynchronous training components to fit staff schedules and enhance feasibility.ConclusionsThis study highlighted the importance of adaptability and evidence-based support in implementing PLIÉ in VA nursing homes. The findings suggest that a flexible, remote training program incorporating both didactic and experiential learning may facilitate the scalability of PLIÉ. Understanding barriers and facilitators can inform strategies to improve the implementation of non-pharmacologic interventions for residents with dementia, ultimately enhancing care quality and outcomes in nursing homes.

title: Distinct amino acid signatures and neutralization sensitivity of plasma- and CSF-derived HIV-1 subtype C clones.
abstract: Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) offer a promising alternative for HIV prevention and treatment, with the potential to cross the blood-brain barrier. However, the extent to which viral genetic variation between the peripheral blood and central nervous system impacts bnAb sensitivity remains insufficiently characterized. This study investigates sequence differences and neutralization profiles of matched plasma- and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)-derived HIV-1 subtype C (HIV-1C) variants in patients coinfected with cryptococcal meningitis. Matched plasma and CSF samples were obtained from seven participants with HIV-cryptococcal meningitis coinfection in Durban, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. HIV-1C env was amplified, cloned into a vector, and sequenced by Sanger sequencing. Amino acid sequences within bnAb epitopes were compared between plasma- and CSF-derived clones. Additionally, we generated Env-pseudotyped viruses and assessed their neutralisation sensitivity using eight bnAbs targeting five known bnAb epitopes on HIV-1 Env. Discordant bnAb escape mutations and variations in neutralization sensitivity between plasma and CSF were observed in the CD4 binding site, V2 Apex and the V3 glycan supersite. Despite these variations, VRC07-523LS demonstrated broad neutralisation activity, with no significant differences in sensitivity across plasma and CSF variants. However, only minor neutralization sensitivity variations were observed in the MPER and gp120-gp41 interface between plasma and CSF compartments. These findings highlight potential differences in amino acid signatures and neutralisation sensitivity between matched plasma- and CSF-derived HIV-1C variants. Our findings show that bnAb targeting the CD4-binding site (VRC07-523LS) maintain cross-compartment efficacy and have a potential in the clearance of viral reservoirs.
keywords: env Gene Products, Human Immunodeficiency Virus

title: Checkpoint-checkpoint combinations in cancer: from mechanistic rationale to translational impact.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors have reshaped the treatment of several cancers, producing durable responses in a subset of patients. However, most individuals either fail to respond or eventually develop resistance. Tumor immune escape results from heterogeneous and often overlapping mechanisms, including impaired antigen presentation, limited T-cell infiltration, co-expression of multiple inhibitory receptors, and suppressive tumor microenvironmental signals. These limitations have driven the development of combination strategies aimed at restoring more effective and sustained antitumor immunity. Among combination approaches, dual immune checkpoint blockade represents the most established strategy. The combination of CTLA-4 and PD-1 inhibitors targets complementary phases of the immune response: early T-cell priming in lymphoid organs and effector function within the tumor microenvironment. Long-term clinical data across melanoma, lung cancer, renal cell carcinoma, mesothelioma, and hepatocellular carcinoma support the ability of this approach to induce durable survival in a meaningful proportion of patients, albeit with increased immune-related toxicity. Building on this foundation, next-generation checkpoint combinations aim to counteract adaptive resistance and T-cell exhaustion. In particular, LAG-3, TIM-3, and TIGIT are frequently co-expressed with programmed death-1 on dysfunctional T cells. Emerging checkpoints such as VISTA, B7-H3, and BTLA further expand the landscape, particularly by modulating myeloid-driven suppression and advanced T-cell dysfunction. In parallel, bispecific antibodies integrating dual checkpoint targeting within a single molecule may enhance coordinated pathway inhibition and tumor localization. Immune checkpoint-based combinations represent an evolving strategy of immune restoration. Future advances will depend on biologically informed trial design, dynamic biomarkers, and rational optimization of dose and sequencing to maximize durable benefit while maintaining acceptable toxicity.
